Variance, Covariance and Correlation: Concepts through Simulation

STAT 400 – Multiple Random Variables

1 The big picture

Quantity Question it answers Formula
Variance How much does one variable bounce around its mean? \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu_X)^2]=E[X^2]-\mu_X^2\)
Covariance When \(X\) is above its mean, is \(Y\) usually above (+) or below (−) its mean? \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]=E[XY]-\mu_X\mu_Y\)
Correlation The same, but with units removed, between \(-1\) and \(1\) \(\rho=\dfrac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\)

Three ideas to keep coming back to:

  1. Covariance and correlation measure linear togetherness only.
  2. Independent \(\Rightarrow\) covariance \(=0\), but not the other way around.
  3. Correlation is not causation.

In each section below we run an experiment, look at the numbers, and interpret them.

2 Variance: one variable bouncing around

Experiment: the number of minutes your bus is late. Two routes have the same average delay (5 minutes) but different reliability.

route_A <- rnorm(10000, mean = 5, sd = 1)   # reliable
route_B <- rnorm(10000, mean = 5, sd = 4)   # unpredictable
data.frame(route = c("A", "B"),
           mean = c(mean(route_A), mean(route_B)),
           variance = c(var(route_A), var(route_B)),
           sd = c(sd(route_A), sd(route_B)))
hist(route_B, breaks = 50, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, .4), xlim = c(-10, 20),
     main = "Bus delay (minutes)", xlab = "minutes late")
hist(route_A, breaks = 50, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .4), add = TRUE)
legend("topright", c("Route A (sd 1)", "Route B (sd 4)"),
       fill = c(rgb(0, 0, 1, .4), rgb(1, 0, 0, .4)), bty = "n")

Interpretation. Same mean, very different variance. The variance is in minutes squared; the standard deviation (the square root) is back in minutes, so we usually quote that.

3 Covariance: do two variables move together?

Experiment: 200 students. \(X\) = hours studied for an exam, \(Y\) = exam score. (Simulated: each extra hour adds about 4 points, plus individual noise.)

n <- 200
hours <- rnorm(n, mean = 6, sd = 2)
score <- 55 + 4 * (hours - 6) + rnorm(n, 0, 8)
head(data.frame(hours = round(hours, 1), score = round(score, 1)))

3.1 The quadrant picture

Draw a vertical line at the average hours and a horizontal line at the average score. The product \((x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)\) is positive (blue) in the upper-right and lower-left quadrants and negative (red) in the other two.

prod_dev <- (hours - mean(hours)) * (score - mean(score))
plot(hours, score, pch = 16, col = ifelse(prod_dev > 0, "blue", "red"),
     xlab = "Hours studied", ylab = "Exam score",
     main = "Blue: product > 0   Red: product < 0")
abline(v = mean(hours), h = mean(score), lty = 2)

Most points are blue, so the average product is positive. That average is the covariance:

sum(prod_dev) / (n - 1)    # sample covariance by hand
## [1] 12.15598
cov(hours, score)          # R's built-in: identical
## [1] 12.15598

Interpretation. A positive covariance means “above-average study time goes with above-average scores”. But what does a covariance of about 12 mean? “Hour-points” is not a natural unit, so we need correlation.

3.2 Seeing different covariances

Same spread for \(X\) and \(Y\) in every panel; only the strength and direction of the relationship change.

sim_pair <- function(rho, n) {
  x <- rnorm(n); y <- rho * x + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)
  cbind(x, y)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 5), mar = c(4, 3, 3, 1))
for (r in c(-0.9, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 0.9)) {
  d <- sim_pair(r, 1000)
  plot(d, pch = 16, cex = .4, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .3), xlim = c(-4, 4), ylim = c(-4, 4),
       main = sprintf("true rho=%.1f\nsample r=%.2f", r, cor(d[, 1], d[, 2])))
  abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 2, col = "red")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

4 Correlation: covariance without units

height_in <- rnorm(300, 68, 3)
weight_lb <- 150 + 4 * (height_in - 68) + rnorm(300, 0, 15)
data.frame(
  units = c("inches & pounds", "centimetres & kilograms"),
  covariance  = c(cov(height_in, weight_lb), cov(height_in * 2.54, weight_lb * 0.4536)),
  correlation = c(cor(height_in, weight_lb), cor(height_in * 2.54, weight_lb * 0.4536)))

Interpretation. Changing units multiplies the covariance by \(2.54\times0.4536\approx1.15\), but the correlation does not move. That is why we compare correlations, not covariances, across different variables. A correlation near \(\pm1\) means a tight straight-line pattern; near 0 means no linear pattern.

5 Experiment: two dice

Roll two fair dice. \(D_1\), \(D_2\) are the dice, \(S=D_1+D_2\), and \(G=|D_1-D_2|\) is the gap. There are only 36 equally likely outcomes, so we can compute everything exactly.

o <- expand.grid(d1 = 1:6, d2 = 1:6)
o$s <- o$d1 + o$d2; o$gap <- abs(o$d1 - o$d2); o$mx <- pmax(o$d1, o$d2)
res <- rbind(
  "D1 and D2"   = c(pop_cov(o$d1, o$d2),  pop_cor(o$d1, o$d2)),
  "D1 and sum"  = c(pop_cov(o$d1, o$s),   pop_cor(o$d1, o$s)),
  "D1 and max"  = c(pop_cov(o$d1, o$mx),  pop_cor(o$d1, o$mx)),
  "sum and gap" = c(pop_cov(o$s, o$gap),  pop_cor(o$s, o$gap)))
colnames(res) <- c("Cov", "Corr"); round(res, 4)
##                Cov   Corr
## D1 and D2   0.0000 0.0000
## D1 and sum  2.9167 0.7071
## D1 and max  1.4583 0.6082
## sum and gap 0.0000 0.0000

Interpretation.

  • D1 and D2: 0. The dice cannot influence each other.
  • D1 and sum: \(\mathrm{Cov}(D_1,D_1+D_2)=\mathrm{Var}(D_1)+0=35/12\approx2.917\), and \(\rho=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707\). Half of the sum’s variance comes from the first die.
  • sum and gap: covariance 0, yet they are not independent:
c(P_joint = mean(o$s == 2 & o$gap == 0),
  P_product = mean(o$s == 2) * mean(o$gap == 0))
##    P_joint  P_product 
## 0.02777778 0.00462963

If the sum is 2, the gap must be 0 (joint probability 1/36), but the product of the marginals is only \((1/36)(6/36)\). Uncorrelated \(\neq\) independent.

Simulating the experiment gives the same story (with sampling noise):

a <- sample(6, 10000, TRUE); b <- sample(6, 10000, TRUE)
c(cor_D1_D2 = cor(a, b), cor_D1_sum = cor(a, a + b))
##    cor_D1_D2   cor_D1_sum 
## 0.0004343469 0.7071772758

6 Experiment: guessing on a true/false quiz

A student guesses all 10 questions. \(X\) = number correct, \(Y\) = number wrong, so \(Y=10-X\).

correct <- rbinom(5000, 10, 0.5); wrong <- 10 - correct
c(cov = cov(correct, wrong), var_correct = var(correct), cor = cor(correct, wrong))
##         cov var_correct         cor 
##   -2.430357    2.430357   -1.000000
plot(jitter(correct), jitter(wrong), pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .15),
     xlab = "# correct", ylab = "# wrong", main = "Perfect negative correlation")

cor(correct, 5 * correct)   # points per question: still +1
## [1] 1

Interpretation. \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,10-X)=-\mathrm{Var}(X)=-2.5\) and \(\rho=-1\) exactly: a perfect decreasing straight line. Multiplying the score by 5 points per question does not change the correlation (+1 with the score).

7 Experiment: dealing two cards

\(X=1\) if the first card is a heart, \(Y=1\) if the second is.

deck <- rep(c(1, 0), c(13, 39))
draw <- function(replace) deck[sample(52, 2, replace = replace)]
wo <- t(replicate(2e5, draw(FALSE)))
w  <- t(replicate(2e5, draw(TRUE)))
data.frame(sampling = c("with replacement", "without replacement"),
           covariance = c(cov(w[, 1], w[, 2]), cov(wo[, 1], wo[, 2])),
           exact = c(0, -1/272))

Interpretation. Without replacement, one heart gone leaves fewer hearts in the deck: a tiny negative dependence (\(\rho=-1/51\approx-0.02\)). Dependence can be real yet weak, and it fades as the population grows, which is why polling 1,000 people from millions behaves almost like independent sampling.

8 Experiment: commute time and rain (why \(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)\) needs covariance)

Your trip is a bus ride \(B\) plus a walk \(W\). It rains with probability 0.3 and rain slows both:

  • \(B=20+10R+\varepsilon_B\), \(\varepsilon_B\sim N(0,3^2)\)
  • \(W=10+6R+\varepsilon_W\), \(\varepsilon_W\sim N(0,2^2)\)
n <- 1e5
rain  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)
bus   <- 20 + 10 * rain + rnorm(n, 0, 3)
walk  <- 10 +  6 * rain + rnorm(n, 0, 2)
total <- bus + walk
c(var_bus = var(bus), var_walk = var(walk), cov = cov(bus, walk), cor = cor(bus, walk))
##    var_bus   var_walk        cov        cor 
## 30.2181565 11.6316363 12.7040346  0.6776217

Theory says \(\mathrm{Cov}(B,W)=10\cdot6\cdot\mathrm{Var}(R)=60(0.21)=12.6\). Now the variance of the total:

data.frame(
  method = c("Var(B)+Var(W)  (pretend independent)",
             "Var(B)+Var(W)+2Cov(B,W)",
             "Simulated Var(B+W)"),
  variance = c(var(bus) + var(walk),
               var(bus) + var(walk) + 2 * cov(bus, walk),
               var(total)))

The second and third lines match; the naive first line is far too small. What does that cost you? Suppose you want to be on time 95% of the time:

c(true_95th_percentile  = unname(quantile(total, .95)),
  naive_independent_95th = mean(total) + qnorm(.95) * sqrt(var(bus) + var(walk)))
##   true_95th_percentile naive_independent_95th 
##               49.51687               45.49620
hist(total, breaks = 60, col = "grey85", main = "Total commute time", xlab = "minutes")

Interpretation. Because rain hits both parts of the trip, bad days are bad on both ends and the total is more spread out (a two-humped distribution: dry days and rainy days). Ignoring covariance gives a buffer that is too small. The same thing happens with money: two stocks that fall together make a riskier portfolio than their separate variances suggest, and two stocks that move oppositely reduce the variance of the sum.

To see the effect of the covariance alone, scramble the walk times so they no longer line up with the bus times (same marginal distributions, link broken):

c(original = var(bus + walk), shuffled = var(bus + sample(walk)))
## original shuffled 
## 67.25786 41.85545

9 Experiment: temperature and electricity use

A house heats when it’s cold and air-conditions when it’s hot. \(X\) = outdoor temperature minus 20°C (uniform on \([-15,15]\)), \(Y\approx|X|\) plus noise.

temp   <- runif(3000, -15, 15)
energy <- abs(temp) + rnorm(3000, 0, 1)
plot(temp, energy, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .25),
     xlab = "Outdoor temp minus 20C", ylab = "Energy use",
     main = sprintf("Strong relationship, correlation = %.2f", cor(temp, energy)))

c(cov = cov(temp, energy), cor = cor(temp, energy))
##        cov        cor 
## 0.47780139 0.01238359

Interpretation. \(Y\) is almost determined by \(X\), yet the correlation is about 0: cold days (negative \(x\)) and hot days (positive \(x\)) both mean high energy use, so the positive and negative products cancel. Always plot the data.

10 A discrete joint distribution, start to finish

For a student, \(X\) = number of late assignments and \(Y\) = number of missed lectures, with joint pmf:

p <- matrix(c(.2, .1, 0,
              .1, .3, .1,
              0,  .1, .1), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(X = 0:2, Y = 0:2))
p
##    Y
## X     0   1   2
##   0 0.2 0.1 0.0
##   1 0.1 0.3 0.1
##   2 0.0 0.1 0.1
vals <- 0:2
c(sum_check = sum(p), marg_X = rowSums(p), marg_Y = colSums(p))
## sum_check  marg_X.0  marg_X.1  marg_X.2  marg_Y.0  marg_Y.1  marg_Y.2 
##       1.0       0.3       0.5       0.2       0.3       0.5       0.2
EX  <- sum(vals * rowSums(p));  EY  <- sum(vals * colSums(p))
EXY <- sum(outer(vals, vals) * p)
covXY <- EXY - EX * EY
varX  <- sum(vals^2 * rowSums(p)) - EX^2
varY  <- sum(vals^2 * colSums(p)) - EY^2
c(EX = EX, EY = EY, EXY = EXY, Cov = covXY, VarX = varX, VarY = varY,
  Corr = covXY / sqrt(varX * varY))
##        EX        EY       EXY       Cov      VarX      VarY      Corr 
## 0.9000000 0.9000000 1.1000000 0.2900000 0.4900000 0.4900000 0.5918367

Check by simulating 100,000 students from the table:

cells <- expand.grid(Y = vals, X = vals)[, c("X", "Y")]       # X slowest, matches t(p)
idx <- sample(nrow(cells), 1e5, replace = TRUE, prob = as.vector(t(p)))
s <- cells[idx, ]
c(cov = cov(s$X, s$Y), cor = cor(s$X, s$Y))
##       cov       cor 
## 0.2905961 0.5924686

Interpretation. \(\mathrm{Cov}=1.1-0.9^2=0.29>0\) and \(\rho\approx0.59\): students with more late assignments tend to miss more lectures. They are dependent: \(P(0,0)=0.2\) but \(p_X(0)p_Y(0)=0.09\).

11 Correlation is not causation

Experiment: daily ice-cream sales and swimming-pool injuries over a summer. Neither causes the other; temperature drives both.

days  <- 120
temp  <- rnorm(days, 28, 5)
icecream <- 50 + 8 * temp + rnorm(days, 0, 25)
injuries <- 1 + 0.25 * temp + rnorm(days, 0, 1.5)
cor(icecream, injuries)                       # clearly positive, and spurious
## [1] 0.5356977
# Adjust for temperature: correlate what is LEFT after removing the temperature effect
cor(resid(lm(icecream ~ temp)), resid(lm(injuries ~ temp)))
## [1] -0.1837386
plot(icecream, injuries, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .4),
     main = "A correlation without causation")

Interpretation. Once the effect of temperature is removed from both variables, the leftover correlation is near 0, which exposes the lurking variable. (Statisticians call this a partial correlation.)

12 Class survey activity (use your own data)

Replace the simulated data below with the class survey (read.csv("survey.csv"): height, shoe, sleep, study).

height <- rnorm(60, 67, 4); shoe <- 0.9 * (height - 67) + 9 + rnorm(60, 0, 0.8)
sleep  <- rnorm(60, 7, 1);  study <- pmax(0, 12 - 0.8 * sleep + rnorm(60, 0, 2))
c(height_shoe = cor(height, shoe), sleep_study = cor(sleep, study))
## height_shoe sleep_study 
##   0.9615218  -0.4191861

Outliers: add one badly recorded data point (a student listed as 7 feet tall with size-7 shoes). Pearson correlation is sensitive to it; the rank-based Spearman correlation moves much less.

c(pearson_before = cor(height, shoe),
  pearson_after  = cor(c(height, 84), c(shoe, 7)),
  spearman_after = cor(c(height, 84), c(shoe, 7), method = "spearman"))
## pearson_before  pearson_after spearman_after 
##      0.9615218      0.7521562      0.9043892

13 Summary

Experiment Cov_sign Lesson
Study hours / score + Quadrants: average product of deviations
Dice: D1 and sum + Part of a variable is shared with the sum
Dice: sum and gap 0 Uncorrelated but dependent
True/false quiz - Perfect linear relation: rho = -1; scale-free
Two cards, no replacement - Small, real dependence
Rain commute + Var(X+Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2 Cov; risk and buffers
Temperature / energy 0 Correlation only sees linear association

14 Practice problems

  1. If \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=4\), \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=9\), \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=3\), find \(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)\), \(\mathrm{Var}(X-Y)\) and \(\rho\). (Answers: 19, 7, 0.5)
  2. In the commute experiment, change the rain probability to 0.1 and 0.5. Which gives the larger covariance between bus and walk? (Use \(\mathrm{Var}(R)=p(1-p)\), then check by simulation.)
  3. Create two variables that are dependent but have correlation near 0 other than \(Y=|X|\).
  4. Two independent stocks each have SD $10. What is the SD of their sum if the correlation is 0? \(+0.8\)? \(-0.8\)? (14.1, 19.0, 6.3)
  5. Using the dice, compute \(\mathrm{Cov}(D_1, \min(D_1,D_2))\) and explain its sign.
